newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Spending spree underway in Mexico asset sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spending spree underway in Mexico asset sale.

text.p: Mexico's first successful bargain sale of bank assets, being auctioned off to recoup losses after a devastating peso crisis, should usher in a shopping spree for buyers of distressed debt, the agency conducting the sale said.

Oscar Medina Mora, director of the Valuation and Sale of Assets (VVA) agency running the auctions for the government, told Reuters late on Thursday that this week's sale of choice bank assets had gone extremely well.

A successful first sale was extremely important for the Mexican government, which is hoping to recoup via subsequent auctions millions of dollars of bad debt which it took onto its books to bail out the banks after peso crashed in December 1994.
Wednesday's sell-off went ahead without a hitch despite protests by citizen debtor groups.
"The process was very well flagged and went ahead, in the words of one banker, in a very smooth fashion," Mora told Reuters in an interview.
"There was a very good number of participants and above all the quality of those who took part was very significant."
Dallas-based Amresco Financial LP carried off 135 million pesos ($17.1 million) in secured and current commercial and industrial loans.
Amresco claimed the portfolio for 66.8 million pesos ($8.5 million) or 49 percent of its value after winning the first auction against 12 local and foreign competitors.
"I believe that by having Amresco there, Mexican and the international community of investors will realise there are very good opportunities to be had," Mora said.

The vast bulk of the assets yet to go under the hammer consist of large scale property and company debt, but it also involves a small amount of family mortgage debt and assets such as cars, artworks and jewelry, used to secure loans.
The strong field of participants will give VVA a boost as it gears up for its next sell-offs.

Mora said a Mexico City office building was next on the agenda, and VVA wants to start selling off at least one of 540 large company credits, each worth at least 50 million pesos ($6.33 million), by the end of July.

VVA is acting on behalf of Fobaproa, a government fund set up to save Mexico's banking sector from collapse after the 1994-95 peso crisis by buying up some 340 billion pesos ($43.2 billion) of distressed bank debt.
That amount of debt is equivalent to 13.36 percent of Mexico's gross domestic product, based on 1996's nominal level of 2,544 billion pesos ($322.03 billion).
Wednesday's auction consisted of a portfolio of 35 best quality credits whose payments were still up-to-date, purchased by Fobaproa along with the banks' overwhelming bad debt portfolios.
It aims to auction assets worth some 15 billion pesos ($1.9 billion) in the months till March and has a hefty program in the wings for the next few years.
But as Wednesday's auction got underway, some 300 demonstrators protested outside Fobaproa's Mexico City offices. saying the process had unfairly excluded the debtors themselves.

Gerardo Fernandez Norona, president of the Citizens' Assembly for Bank Debtors, said the auctions aimed to circumvent Mexico's strong constitutional protection for property-owners' rights by selling on their debt to third parties.
"The auctions are illegal and illegitimate," he said. "We are asking them not to conduct the auctions without offering the debt to us at secondary market prices."
The group has held talks with Fobaproa management and has agreed to wait eight days for a response.
"If not, there will be a strong confrontation, we will use civil disobediance, with demonstrations and picketing," he said. ((Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905))
